Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation

Xuyuan Xiong    Siyu Chen    Zihan Shao    Yue Su    Weiyang Jin    Ping Luo    Zhuoran Yang    Xihui Liu
Abstract

Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with BPTT (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, although this may weaken the benefit of looping. To study this tradeoff systematically, we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

1  Introduction

Looped transformers have attracted attention for combining strong performance with efficient use of parameters and training memory. By repeatedly applying a shared block of layers, they increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025). To reduce the cost of training these repeated blocks, several looped language models use truncated BPTT (BPTT), propagating gradients only through the final loops while executing the earlier loops without tracking gradients (Geiping et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026). Truncation introduces a new tradeoff: it saves backward computation and activation memory during training but can weaken the gains from looping (Schwethelm et al., 2026). To achieve the best performance under a fixed training compute budget, we must therefore decide how to divide compute among forward loops, backward loops, model size, and training tokens.

Existing scaling studies examine prescribed backpropagation recipes rather than jointly modeling forward and backward loop counts. Schwethelm et al. (2026) compare full BPTT with truncation to half the loops, fitting a separate scaling law to each recipe. Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026) varies backward-loop counts in small-model experiments but fixes them to half the forward-loop count in its scaling study, leaving their joint optimization to future work. These studies characterize specific recipes but do not provide a unified law for choosing both loop counts across model sizes and token budgets (Table 1). We thus ask:

How do model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loops jointly affect loss, and should we truncate backpropagation under a fixed training compute budget?

To characterize how these quantities affect loss, we conduct nearly 600 training runs, including a scaling suite spanning 58M–919M non-embedding parameters, over three orders of magnitude in training tokens per parameter, and up to 16 forward loops. We independently vary forward and backward loop counts across model sizes and token budgets and fit a unified scaling law. The law expresses the benefit of looping through an effective parameter count—the size of a non-looped model that achieves the same loss at the same token budget. Fully trained loops increase the effective parameter count with diminishing returns, while truncation discounts this gain.

We then use the law to decide whether to truncate, and the answer depends on whether the forward-loop count is prescribed. When it is, the law recovers the benefit of truncation reported in prior work (Schwethelm et al., 2026): the saved backward compute supports a larger model and more training tokens, which more than offset the discounted loop gain. When both loop counts can be chosen, however, the law favors full BPTT. Reducing the forward-loop count frees compute for additional backward loops until every remaining loop is trained, and under the fitted law this reallocation yields more effective parameters at the same compute than the original truncated setting. Separately fitted laws and matched-compute experiments support this advantage (Section 5).

Building on this preference for full BPTT, we additionally study how to allocate compute among loop count, training tokens, and model size. Consider first a setting where model size is predetermined, for example due to device memory constraints. At fixed model size, increasing the loop count is an effective way to increase the effective parameter count; however, additional loops offer diminishing gains while increasing the cost per token. The law precisely characterizes the optimal tradeoff between loop count and training tokens, allocating most additional compute to tokens and increasing the loop count only slowly. This result extends Parcae’s fixed-size allocation analysis (Prairie et al., 2026) beyond a prescribed truncation rule. When model size is also free, compute can instead support more unique parameters; under our leading-FLOP approximation, the law favors a non-looped model and identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. In experiments, models with two fully trained loops nearly match compute-optimal non-looped models at equal training compute while having substantially fewer non-embedding parameters. With a little more training compute, such a smaller model surpasses the compute-optimal non-looped model (Section 6).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A unified scaling law based on effective parameters. We develop and validate a law that expresses loop gains and truncation discounts through an effective parameter count, jointly modeling model size, training tokens, and independent forward and backward loop counts (Section 4).

  • •

    An explanation of when truncation pays. We show why truncation can pay at a prescribed forward-loop count and why joint forward–backward allocation favors full BPTT under the fitted law, supported by matched-compute experiments (Section 5).

  • •

    Compute-allocation rules and parameter-efficient training. We derive allocation rules for fixed and free model size and demonstrate that two fully trained loops nearly match compute-optimal non-looped models while having substantially fewer trainable parameters (Section 6).

Figure 1 previews the three results: loops add effective parameters and truncation discounts them; at fixed model size the best loop count grows with compute; two fully trained loops match the loss of a non-looped model with fewer parameters for a little more compute.

2  Related work

Looped transformers.

Depth-wise parameter sharing in Universal Transformers and ALBERT decouples computational depth from the number of trainable parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2019). Theoretical and controlled studies show how recurrence supports iterative programs, in-context learning algorithms, and depth-sensitive reasoning (Giannou et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Saunshi et al., 2025). In language model pretraining, Huginn uses a prelude–recurrent–coda architecture (Geiping et al., 2025), while Ouro scales looped pretraining to 7.7T tokens (Zhu et al., 2025). Other work adds recurrence to pretrained models (Bae et al., 2025a; McLeish et al., 2025) or adapts depth at inference (Bae et al., 2025b; Jeddi et al., 2026). Recent architectures improve recurrence through residual and hyper-connections (Prairie et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Marchenko et al., 2026; Zeitoun et al., 2026) or MoE routing (Csordás et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). These studies show that looping improves parameter efficiency across architectures; we instead fix the architecture and ask how to train its loops and allocate compute.

Training through recurrent depth.

Truncated BPTT limits gradient propagation to a subset of recurrent steps, saving activation memory and backward compute at the cost of biased gradients (Williams and Peng, 1990; Tallec and Ollivier, 2017). Looped language models often supervise the final output and backpropagate through only the last few loops: Huginn and retrofitted models use at most eight backward steps (Geiping et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025). Hierarchical recurrent models likewise use a short backward horizon (Wang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a). Other approaches use implicit differentiation (Bai et al., 2019), fixed-point gradient approximations (Huang et al., 2026), or supervision within recurrent segments (He et al., 2026). In these recipes the backward depth is fixed; we vary it independently of the forward depth, weighing the compute that truncation saves against the loop gain it costs.

Scaling laws for recurrence.

Size–data scaling laws quantify how parameters and training tokens jointly determine loss (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Videau et al., 2026), and their compute-optimal predictions depend on how the laws are fitted and compute is counted (Besiroglu et al., 2024; Porian et al., 2024; Pearce and Song, 2024; Choshen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a). Extensions account for architectural choices such as MoE sparsity (Clark et al., 2022; Krajewski et al., 2024; Abnar et al., 2025). For looped models, some laws fit each architecture separately (Wang et al., 2026b; Lee et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026c), while others model the loop count explicitly (Table 1) through additive loss terms (Zhu et al., 2025) or effective parameters with linear, power-law, or bounded gains (Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b). Among these scaling-law studies of looped transformers, Iso-Depth (Schwethelm et al., 2026) and Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026) are particularly related to our work. Iso-Depth fits separate laws for full and half-length backpropagation and finds that truncation weakens the loop gain but lowers the loss at a fixed forward-loop count by freeing compute. At fixed model size, Parcae finds that loops and tokens should grow together with compute, but ties the backward loops to half the forward loops and leaves their joint choice open. Our law instead treats the backward-loop count as a separate variable, combining coupled size–data scaling (Videau et al., 2026) with bounded loop gains (Chen et al., 2026b). It recovers the truncation benefit at a prescribed forward-loop count but favors full BPTT when both counts are free (Section 5). In looped MoE models, two loops are the common choice (He et al., 2026): SMELT finds them better than three or four under matched budgets (Wang et al., 2026b), and Loopie finds the marginal benefit of recurrence largest at two (Gao et al., 2026). For dense models, our law ranks two fully trained loops first among looped settings, since they provide nearly the effective size of two untied copies of the block while further loops add less (Section 6.2). In our runs, two-loop models nearly match compute-optimal models without looping at equal compute while having substantially fewer non-embedding parameters (Section 6.3).

3  Preliminaries

Looped transformers.

We study the prelude–recurrent–coda architecture (Geiping et al., 2025; Schwethelm et al., 2026) (Section A.2), which places a shared recurrent block ℛ\mathcal{R} (ℓr\ell_{r} layers) between a prelude 𝒫\mathcal{P} (ℓp\ell_{p} layers, including the input embedding) and a coda 𝒞\mathcal{C} (ℓc\ell_{c} layers, including the output head); see Figure 1a and Appendix A (Figure 10). (3.1)

Here all hidden states have width dd, [s0;st−1][\,s_{0}\,;\,s_{t-1}\,] concatenates the prelude output with the previous state, Winj∈ℝd×2​dW_{\mathrm{inj}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 2d} projects it back to width dd, and the cross-entropy loss applies only to the final output distribution pp. We split the non-embedding parameters NN into N=Nonce+NrecN=N_{\mathrm{once}}+N_{\mathrm{rec}}, where NonceN_{\mathrm{once}} counts 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} (run once per token) and NrecN_{\mathrm{rec}} counts ℛ\mathcal{R} and WinjW_{\mathrm{inj}} (reused each loop; Table 4).

Loop settings, full BPTT, and truncated BPTT.

A loop setting (T,B)(T,B) with 1≤B≤T1\leq B\leq T executes TT forward loops and backpropagates gradients through only the last BB loops (Figure 1a). During training, the state sT−Bs_{T-B} is detached from the computation graph, so the first T−BT-B loops run without gradients; because s0s_{0} is injected at every loop in (3.1), the prelude 𝒫\mathcal{P} retains a direct gradient path for any B≥1B\geq 1. Thus B=TB=T gives full BPTT, B<TB<T gives truncated BPTT, and (1,1)(1,1) recovers a standard non-looped transformer.

Baseline scaling law.

To relate validation loss to non-embedding parameter count NN and training tokens DD for a non-looped model, we adopt the coupled scaling law of Videau et al. (2026),

L⁡(N,D)=E+[A​(NN0)−α+H​(DD0)−β]κ,L(N,D)\;=\;E+\Bigl[A\Bigl(\frac{N}{N_{0}}\Bigr)^{-\alpha}+H\Bigl(\frac{D}{D_{0}}\Bigr)^{-\beta}\Bigr]^{\kappa}, (3.2)

where EE is the irreducible loss, N0N_{0} and D0D_{0} are fixed reference scales (we give token budgets in units of D0=230D_{0}=2^{30} tokens), α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 are the size and token exponents, and the outer exponent κ\kappa couples the two terms (κ=1\kappa=1 recovers the additive form of Hoffmann et al. (2022)); we denote the data coefficient by HH to reserve BB for backward loops. Section 4 extends (3.2) to looped models by replacing NN with an effective parameter count in which (T,B)(T,B) rescales NrecN_{\mathrm{rec}} by a looping coefficient g⁡(T,B)g(T,B).

4  A scaling law for forward and backward loops

Should a looped transformer truncate backpropagation? At a fixed model size and training compute, truncation saves backward computation that can be spent on more forward loops or more training data, but it also reduces the benefit of looping. We fit a scaling law that separates forward and backward loop counts to quantify this tradeoff. This section fits and validates the law and interprets it in terms of effective parameters. Section 5 then uses the law to decide whether to truncate, and Section 6 uses it to divide compute among loops, data, and model size.

4.1  Fitting and validating the scaling law

Experimental setup.

We follow the architecture and training recipe of Schwethelm et al. (2026), using the prelude–recurrent–coda layout of Section 3. We train a grid of five model sizes from 58M to 919M non-embedding parameters (Table 4) on the 100B-token FineWeb-Edu corpus (Penedo et al., 2024). We use MuonH for transformer-block and input-injection matrices and AdamW for embedding, output, and normalization parameters (Jordan et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025). We report validation cross-entropy in nats per token on deduplicated held-out shards; Section A.2 gives the full training and evaluation setup, including the learning-rate and batch-size rules.

Our 592 training runs include a scaling suite of 347 distinct configurations spanning 1.1–1,291 tokens per parameter and fifteen (T,B)(T,B) combinations with T∈{1,2,4,8,16}T\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}, keeping each model’s parameter count fixed (Prairie et al., 2026). We fit the law on 230 configurations and reserve 117 for separate tests. For configurations with multiple accepted runs, we use their mean validation loss. Each configuration receives the same weight in the fit, regardless of its number of runs. Other experiments cover compute allocation, comparisons with untied models, learning-rate sweeps, and batch-size sweeps; Sections A.2, B.3, D and E give the full experimental design and fitting details.

Effective-parameter scaling law.

Only the recurrent block runs in every loop, so looping can enlarge only this block. We therefore write the loss as the coupled law of Videau et al. (2026) with an effective parameter count. In it, the recurrent block, NrecN_{\mathrm{rec}}, counts several times, and the prelude and coda, NonceN_{\mathrm{once}}, count once (Section 3):

L=E+[A​(NeffN0)−α+H​(DD0)−β]κ,Neff=Nonce+g(T,B)Nrec,g(T,B)=exp[c(1−T−pB−q)].\begin{gathered}L=E+\Bigl[A\Bigl(\frac{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}{N_{0}}\Bigr)^{-\alpha}+H\Bigl(\frac{D}{D_{0}}\Bigr)^{-\beta}\Bigr]^{\kappa},\\ N_{\mathrm{eff}}=N_{\mathrm{once}}+g(T,B)N_{\mathrm{rec}},\qquad g(T,B)=\exp\bigl[c\,(1-T^{-p}B^{-q})\bigr].\end{gathered} (4.1)

Here g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) is the looping coefficient: it multiplies the recurrent block’s parameter count, while the prelude and coda count once. With full BPTT, the looping coefficient g⁡(T,T)=exp⁡[c⁡(1−T−(p+q))]g(T,T)=\exp[c(1-T^{-(p+q)})] grows with TT; truncation multiplies it by g⁡(T,B)/g⁡(T,T)≤1g(T,B)/g(T,T)\leq 1.

Design of the looping coefficient.

We choose g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) to satisfy four modeling requirements:

The finite-ceiling assumption is supported by prior observations of saturation: Chen et al. (2026b) model a bounded effective-parameter gain from looping, while Parcae finds that adding test-time loops to a trained model approaches a loss floor (Prairie et al., 2026). There is also an information-storage motivation. At a fixed parameter count and weight precision, the weights can store only a finite amount of information; additional loops provide more computation over those weights without increasing their storage capacity. We therefore treat saturation as an empirical modeling assumption and learn its ceiling from the data.

These requirements motivate the form in (4.1). Nonnegativity motivates an exponential parameterization, ensuring g⁡(T,B)>0g(T,B)>0 for T,B>0T,B>0. With c,p,q>0c,p,q>0, increasing either loop count decreases T−p​B−qT^{-p}B^{-q}, so g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) grows toward the finite ceiling ece^{c}. The shared coefficient cc enforces g⁡(1,1)=1g(1,1)=1, and continuous extension as B→0+B\to 0^{+} gives g⁡(T,0)=0g(T,0)=0. At fixed model size and token budget, pp governs the loss reduction from extra forward loops at fixed BB, while qq governs the loss reduction from extra backward loops at fixed TT. These three loop coefficients, c,p,qc,p,q, together with the six coefficients E,A,H,α,β,κE,A,H,\alpha,\beta,\kappa of the coupled size–data law (3.2), give nine fitted coefficients.

Empirical looping coefficients.

Figure 3 motivates coupling TT and BB: the empirical looping coefficient has a smaller fitted log–log slope against r=B/Tr=B/T at larger TT. Figure 3 compares the shared looping-coefficient surface with empirical looping coefficients. For each looped run with loss ℓ\ell, we first use shape-preserving piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation (PCHIP) (Fritsch and Butland, 1984) to interpolate the non-looped measurements at the same target token budget to obtain the effective size Nwidehateff\widehat{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} matching ℓ\ell. We then use the effective-size relation in (4.1): subtracting NonceN_{\mathrm{once}} and dividing by NrecN_{\mathrm{rec}} gives the empirical looping coefficient gwidehat\widehat{g} (Section B.2). Vertical segments join each empirical median to the fitted coefficient at the same loop setting. This agreement shows that g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) with just three parameters c,p,qc,p,q captures the observed loop dependence; Table 4 quantifies the law’s in-sample fit and leave-one-out (LOO) prediction errors.

Fitting procedure.

We fit all nine parameters jointly by minimizing the sum of squared differences between predicted and measured validation losses, giving each configuration equal weight. The reference scales N0=2.4×108N_{0}=2.4\times 10^{8} parameters and D0=230D_{0}=2^{30} tokens are held fixed. Predictions use actual token counts DD; budget holdouts group target token budgets. To reduce sensitivity to the initial guess, we fit the law 64 times from different random starting values and retain the solution with the smallest fitting error. All fits converge. Table 2 gives the parameters fitted on the 230 configurations used for the validation below. Further fitting details are in Appendix B.

Holdout validation.

To test whether the law predicts measurements it has not been fitted to, we leave out selected configurations, fit all nine parameters again using the remaining measurements, and compare the predictions with the omitted measurements. For example, to test prediction at an unseen model size, we exclude every configuration at that size and fit the law using the other sizes. We repeat this for each size and for the other exclusions listed in Table 4.

Prediction accuracy.

The law tracks the measured loss curves across sizes and token budgets (Figure 4), including the held-out configurations (marked with open circles). Figure 5 gives the complementary view across loop settings at a fixed model size and token budget: varying TT with B=TB=T, varying BB at fixed TT, and varying TT at fixed BB. Both figures use the law fitted on the 230-configuration fitting set; the curves are evaluated on both fitted and held-out configurations. Appendix F overlays the law on the five-size grid of the scaling suite.

Holding out a model size or token budget increases prediction error only modestly (Table 4), whereas unseen loop settings are harder to predict (Appendix B). Extrapolation back to the non-looped baseline is the weakest loop-count check; Appendix B reports the boundary errors and alternative gains. The table separates fit quality from held-out prediction error. Section 4.2 examines the remaining discrepancies in effective-parameter units (Figure 6), and Section 6.1 checks their effect on compute allocation (Figure 8).

4.2  Illustrating the scaling law with effective parameters

How many parameters is a loop setting worth? (4.1) allows us to decompose the answer into the gain from fully trained loops, g⁡(T,T)g(T,T), and the discount for truncation, g⁡(T,B)/g⁡(T,T)g(T,B)/g(T,T). We use the empirical looping coefficients introduced above to compare the law with the runs in Figure 6; their construction is detailed in Section B.2.

The looping coefficient saturates for large TT.

With full BPTT, B=TB=T, and the gain is g⁡(T,T)=exp⁡[c⁡(1−T−(p+q))]g(T,T)=\exp[c(1-T^{-(p+q)})]. The runs in Figure 5a vary both loop counts together at fixed model size and token budget. Each doubling of trained loops adds less than the one before (Figures 5a and 6a), as Chen et al. (2026b) also find with all loops trained. The power-law gain of prior work (Schwethelm et al., 2026) keeps growing, whereas ours approaches ece^{c}. Our runs support the bounded form over the power law, predicting held-out forward-loop counts more accurately (Section B.4).

Doubling BB outweighs doubling TT alone.

At fixed TT, truncation reduces BB and hence g⁡(T,B)g(T,B), consistent with the smaller effective sizes in Figure 6b and higher losses in Figure 5b. Figure 6c clarifies the relative roles of TT and BB by grouping settings with the same BB. The fitted bars and empirical estimates change relatively little as TT increases within a group, but show larger gains as BB increases across groups, including comparisons at the same TT. The fitted exponents quantify this asymmetry: q>pq>p (Table 2) implies g⁡(T,2​B)>g⁡(2​T,B)g(T,2B)>g(2T,B) for 2​B≤T2B\leq T. From the same initial setting at fixed model size, doubling BB thus adds more effective parameters than doubling TT alone; the small loss gains from extra forward loops at fixed BB support the same conclusion (Figure 5c).

5  Truncate or not?

Truncation saves backward compute but reduces the effective parameter count (Section 4.2). Whether it lowers loss at a given compute depends on which quantities are held fixed. We first fix the forward-loop count, as prior scaling studies do, and then let both loop counts vary at equal compute.

5.1  Fixed forward loops: truncation can be optimal

Fix TT and optimize N,D,BN,D,B at compute CC with fixed parameter proportions. The effective size is Neff=Nonce+g⁡(T,B)​NrecN_{\mathrm{eff}}=N_{\mathrm{once}}+g(T,B)N_{\mathrm{rec}}, and the compute-equivalent size NcompN_{\mathrm{comp}} sets the leading cost:

C≃6​D​Ncomp,Ncomp=Nonce+T+2​B3​Nrec.C\simeq 6DN_{\mathrm{comp}},\qquad N_{\mathrm{comp}}=N_{\mathrm{once}}+\frac{T+2B}{3}N_{\mathrm{rec}}. (5.1)

This counts two FLOPs per parameter per forward pass and four per backward pass, omitting attention products, the output projection, and optimizer updates. Under this approximation, Lemma C.1 in Section C.4 shows that optimizing the law over unrestricted positive, continuous N,DN,D reduces to

B∗∈arg​minB∈{1,…,T}⁡χ​(T,B),whereχ⁡(T,B)=NcompNeff.B^{*}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{B\in\{1,\ldots,T\}}\chi(T,B),\qquad\text{where}\quad\chi(T,B)=\frac{N_{\mathrm{comp}}}{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}. (5.2)

Smaller χ\chi means less compute per effective parameter; its ranking is independent of CC under these assumptions. The stationary condition (C.14) gives continuous candidates for B∗B^{*}; integer choices are evaluated directly using χ\chi (Table 6).

Truncation reduces effective size, but frees compute for a larger model and more tokens. At T=8T=8, the law selects B∗=2B^{*}=2 and predicts a 34% compute saving at equal optimized loss (Table 6). Separately fitted laws at T=4,8T=4,8 also favor B=2B=2 over B=TB=T: at T=8T=8, their compute-optimal frontiers predict a 33–35% saving within the range of the runs (Figure 6; fitting details in Section C.4).

This agrees with the fixed-compute truncation benefit reported by Schwethelm et al. (2026). Parcae uses truncated BPTT but leaves the compute-optimal choice of forward and backward loop counts to future work (Prairie et al., 2026, Appendix I). The benefit is conditional on prescribing TT. We next ask whether it survives when both loop counts can be chosen.

5.2  Free forward-loop count: full BPTT is optimal

When TT can also be chosen, we optimize the split between forward and backward loops at equal compute. Fix the model architecture and token count DD. In our FLOP accounting, each forward pass through the recurrent block costs one unit and each backward pass costs two, including their attention operations (Section C.1). The recurrent block thus costs T+2​BT+2B units per token; all other model components have the same cost across loop settings. Holding T+2​BT+2B fixed therefore holds total compute fixed: for example, (T,B)=(4,4)(T,B)=(4,4) and (8,2)(8,2) both cost 12 recurrent units per token.

Under our scaling law, for a loop-compute count S≥3S\geq 3, minimizing loss at this compute is equivalent to maximizing the looping coefficient g⁡(T,B)g(T,B):

maximizeT,B∈ℝg⁡(T,B)subject toT+2​B=S,1≤B≤T.\underset{T,B\in\mathbb{R}}{\operatorname{maximize}}\quad g(T,B)\qquad\text{subject to}\quad T+2B=S,\quad 1\leq B\leq T. (5.3)
The optimal split uses full BPTT.

Recall that g⁡(T,B)=exp⁡[c⁡(1−T−p​B−q)]g(T,B)=\exp[c(1-T^{-p}B^{-q})] with c>0c>0. Thus (5.3) is equivalent to minimizing T−p​B−qT^{-p}B^{-q} under the same affine constraints. This is a standard convex optimization problem: whenever q>2​pq>2p, its unique solution is T=B=S/3T=B=S/3 for every S≥3S\geq 3, giving full BPTT (Lemma C.2 in Section C.4.2). The fitted exponents in Table 2, p≃0.237p\simeq 0.237 and q≃1.022q\simeq 1.022, satisfy q>2​p≃0.474q>2p\simeq 0.474 by a wide margin. Therefore, the law predicts that full BPTT is optimal at every compute if both TT and BB can be chosen continuously.11 1 The fully trained replacement may not be an integer setting: (4,3)(4,3) would become (10/3,10/3)(10/3,10/3). On our integer menu, the law gives (4,3)(4,3) a lead over both (2,2)(2,2) and (4,4)(4,4) of at most 0.002 nats over a narrow compute range, while in the runs the best fully trained setting beats the best truncated one at every size and compute (Figure 8).

Separately fitted laws confirm the benefit of full BPTT.

The compute-optimal frontiers of the separately fitted laws predict that (4,4)(4,4) reaches the same loss with less compute than (8,2)(8,2) where both optimal allocations lie within the ranges of their runs (Figure 8). Matched-compute runs agree: at D=16​D0D=16D_{0}, (4,4)(4,4) achieves lower loss than (8,2)(8,2) at every size (Table 8).

6  Allocating compute among loops, data, and model size

Given full BPTT, it remains to divide training compute among loops, tokens, and model size. Following Hoffmann et al. (2022), we summarize each allocation by how its optimum scales with compute, X∗∝CaX^{*}\propto C^{a}. We first fix the model size (Section 6.1) and then let it vary (Sections 6.2 and 6.3).

6.1  Fixed model size: loops versus data

Suppose a model must fit within a device’s memory budget, so adding parameters is not an option. With more training compute available, should we reuse those parameters through more loops per token, or train on more tokens? At fixed size, more loops raise effective size but leave fewer training tokens within the same compute budget; our law balances these two.

Asymptotic loop–token allocation under full BPTT.

The allocation power laws below describe the large-compute limit of our fitted loss law, not a separate fit to measured optima. Fix the architecture and parameter counts (Nrec>0N_{\mathrm{rec}}>0); setting B=TB=T in (4.1) gives the full-BPTT loss

LN​(T,D)=E+[A​(Nonce+Nrec​ec⁡(1−T−(p+q))N0)−α+H​(DD0)−β]κ.L_{N}(T,D)=E+\left[A\left(\frac{N_{\mathrm{once}}+N_{\mathrm{rec}}e^{c(1-T^{-(p+q)})}}{N_{0}}\right)^{-\alpha}+H\left(\frac{D}{D_{0}}\right)^{-\beta}\right]^{\kappa}. (6.1)

Because κ>0\kappa>0, minimizing (6.1) is equivalent to minimizing its inner sum, JN=(LN−E)1/κJ_{N}=(L_{N}-E)^{1/\kappa}. As T→∞T\to\infty, the effective size approaches N∞=Nonce+ec​NrecN_{\infty}=N_{\mathrm{once}}+e^{c}N_{\mathrm{rec}}. Expanding around this limit gives

JN​(T,D)=J∞+KN​T−(p+q)+H​(DD0)−β+O⁡(T−2​(p+q)),J_{N}(T,D)=J_{\infty}+K_{N}T^{-(p+q)}+H\left(\frac{D}{D_{0}}\right)^{-\beta}+O\!\left(T^{-2(p+q)}\right), (6.2)

where J∞=A​(N∞/N0)−αJ_{\infty}=A(N_{\infty}/N_{0})^{-\alpha} and KN=α​c​(Nrec​ec/N∞)​J∞>0K_{N}=\alpha c(N_{\mathrm{rec}}e^{c}/N_{\infty})J_{\infty}>0 are fixed by the architecture and fitted coefficients; the leading loop term has exponent p+qp+q and the data term has exponent β\beta.

Following the power-law allocation argument of Hoffmann et al. (2022), we balance these two terms under a compute constraint. At fixed size, compute per token grows linearly with TT at large depth (C∝T​DC\propto TD). For continuous T,DT,D, minimizing the leading terms in (6.2) gives the asymptotic scaling

T∗∝Cββ+p+q,D∗∝Cp+qβ+p+qat fixed N.T^{*}\propto C^{\frac{\beta}{\beta+p+q}},\qquad D^{*}\propto C^{\frac{p+q}{\beta+p+q}}\quad\text{at fixed }N. (6.3)

These powers need not describe finite-compute optima, where overheads and integer loop counts remain consequential. Section C.4.3 derives this limit from the exact stationary condition, including the compute overhead of the non-recurrent layers.

Loops grow slowly; most added compute goes to data.

Substituting the fitted p+q≃1.259p+q\simeq 1.259 and β≃0.393\beta\simeq 0.393 into (6.3) gives, with rounded exponents,

T∗∝C0.24,D∗∝C0.76.T^{*}\propto C^{0.24},\qquad D^{*}\propto C^{0.76}. (6.4)

A tenfold increase in compute therefore raises the optimal loop count by about 1.7 times and the token count by about 5.8 times. These exponents are asymptotic: because loop counts are integers, the best setting changes in steps. Between steps, added compute goes to tokens; at each step, the model switches to a deeper setting with fewer tokens. The runs show the same trend: at each size, the loop count minimizing loss at equal compute grows with compute as predicted (Figure 7a–c).

Comparison with prior scaling laws.

Parcae reports empirical exponents of approximately 0.40 for mean recurrence and 0.78 for training tokens (Prairie et al., 2026, Section 5.2). (6.4) agrees that tokens grow faster than loops, but predicts slower loop growth in the asymptotic regime. Parcae samples recurrence and uses truncated BPTT, so its reported optimum is conditional on that training recipe. Our full-BPTT result suggests that truncation may be suboptimal when both loop counts are free under our law and compute model; whether this also holds for Parcae requires a direct comparison. The law of Schwethelm et al. (2026) instead lets the looping coefficient grow unbounded as TφT^{\varphi}. Our gain saturates, and p+qp+q governs the approach to that ceiling, giving a different asymptotic allocation between loops and tokens.

6.2  Free model size: the law favors no looping

When model size is free, the compute spent repeating a block can instead train more unique parameters. Start with a TT-loop model using full BPTT, for integer T≥2T\geq 2, and replace its shared recurrent block with TT untied copies. The resulting non-looped model has the same compute CC and token budget DD under (5.1), but greater effective size:

Nonce+g⁡(T,T)​Nrec<Nonce+T​Nrec.N_{\mathrm{once}}+g(T,T)N_{\mathrm{rec}}<N_{\mathrm{once}}+TN_{\mathrm{rec}}. (6.5)

The left side is the effective size of the looped model; the right side is that of the model with TT untied copies. The inequality follows from the fitted g⁡(T,T)<Tg(T,T)<T (Figure 9; Section C.4.4). The non-looped model therefore has greater effective size and lower predicted loss at every token budget. Figure 9 also shows that g⁡(2,2)g(2,2) is close to 22; we examine this two-loop case in detail in Section 6.3.

The best loop setting does not change with compute.

With parameter proportions fixed and positive, continuous N,DN,D unrestricted, every loop setting shares the compute exponents of the model without looping. Optimizing the loop setting as well gives

N∗∝C0.56,D∗∝C0.44,T∗=B∗=1.N^{*}\propto C^{0.56},\qquad D^{*}\propto C^{0.44},\qquad T^{*}=B^{*}=1. (6.6)

The exponents are rounded predictions under the leading-FLOP count (Section C.4.4). Under these assumptions, the ranking of loop settings is the same at every compute.

No looping is optimal, and two fully trained loops come closest.

Among the fifteen settings, the law favors the model without looping at fixed compute, consistent with Schwethelm et al. (2026). The best looped setting is (2,2)(2,2) (Table 6): g⁡(2,2)≈2g(2,2)\approx 2, so two shared loops provide nearly the effective size of two untied copies. Because Neff>NN_{\mathrm{eff}}>N for (2,2)(2,2), the law predicts that it comes close to the model without looping while having fewer trainable parameters. Section 6.3 tests this prediction.

6.3  Two fully trained loops are competitive with fewer parameters

Near parity at equal compute.

At each of three training budgets, we train a model with two fully trained loops, (2,2)(2,2), and a model without looping, each at the size and token count that minimize its loss for that budget, with three seeds per model (Appendix D). At every budget, the looped model stays within 0.008 nats of the model without looping while having 27–32% fewer non-embedding parameters (Table 13). The gap shrinks as the budget grows, and at 2.1×10192.1\times 10^{19} FLOPs22 2 Including the optimizer update, as in Table 13; the forward and backward passes alone take 2.0×10192.0\times 10^{19} FLOPs. it is smaller than its standard error across seeds. Both models sit near the flat minima of their IsoFLOP profiles, the looped one at a smaller size (Figure 7d).

Ahead with a little more compute.

Because the gap is so small, a little more compute lets the looped model pull ahead. We take the pair at 2.1×10192.1\times 10^{19} FLOPs and train its (2,2)(2,2) model on 8% more tokens, and so with 8% more compute. Its loss then falls 0.007 nats below that of the model without looping, well beyond the spread across seeds, while it still has 27% fewer non-embedding parameters (Figure 1d; Table 13). Appendix D also compares the looped model with an untied model, which gives each loop its own block, at a fixed number of training tokens.

7  Conclusion

Truncated BPTT saves compute, but whether it lowers the loss depends on which quantities are held fixed. We fit a scaling law that expresses every loop setting as effective parameters, with a gain that saturates and shrinks under truncation (Section 4). Under this law, truncation helps only when the forward-loop count is prescribed. When both loop counts are chosen, full BPTT is optimal at every model size and compute we analyze (Section 5).

The law also determines how to allocate compute. At fixed model size, most additional compute should go to data, and the number of fully trained loops grows only as about C0.24C^{0.24} (Section 6.1). When model size is free, the law favors no looping, but two fully trained loops come close: with 27–32% fewer non-embedding parameters they nearly match the compute-optimal non-looped model at equal compute, and with 27% fewer parameters they achieve lower loss at 8% more compute (Section 6.3).

Limitations.

Our main limitation is the focus on dense models: we do not study mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, so whether our conclusions on truncation and compute allocation extend to looped MoE models remains open. Second, we measure validation loss only and do not establish whether the observed gains translate to downstream task performance or reasoning ability. Third, our experiments are capped at T≤16T\leq 16, so the gain ceiling and later switches to more loops remain extrapolations. Related scaling sweeps reach eight loops in Schwethelm et al. (2026) and mean training loop counts of twelve in Parcae (Prairie et al., 2026). Much deeper recurrence can exacerbate training instability, including residual explosion and loss spikes (Prairie et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026); developing stable training recipes for that regime is beyond our scope. Finally, we fix the ratio of non-embedding parameters in the combined prelude and coda to those in the recurrent block for each model size. Varying this ratio to study how parameter allocation affects the gains from looping and the compute-optimal loop counts is a direction for future work.

Appendix A Model architecture and experimental setup

A.1  Model architecture

Figure 10 draws the model of Section 3 for the loop setting (4,2)(4,2). In a training step (Figure 10a), the prelude maps the tokens to e=s0e=s_{0}, every loop reads ee again through the input injection, and the state sT−Bs_{T-B} entering the last BB loops is treated as a constant. The gradient therefore reaches the coda, the last BB loops and, through the injection, the prelude; the first T−BT-B loops run forward only, and evaluation runs all TT loops. Each loop (Figure 10b) applies WinjW_{\mathrm{inj}} to [e;st−1][\,e\,;\,s_{t-1}\,], the ℓr\ell_{r} pre-norm transformer layers of RR and an RMSNorm, with the same weights in every loop. At 2 FLOPs per parameter and token for a forward pass and 4 for a backward pass (Figure 10c), the prelude and coda cost 6, each forward loop 2 and each backward loop 4 more, which gives approximately N⁡(3+T+2​B)N(3+T+2B) FLOPs per token under our parameter split, before attention and output costs (C.1); the optimizer update adds a cost per step (C.3).

A.2  Experimental setup

Models.

We take the architecture and the training recipe of Schwethelm et al. (2026), the reference recipe below, which builds on the prelude–recurrent–coda layout of Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) (Section 3). Its blocks use pre-norm attention with query–key normalization and rotary position embeddings, head dimension 128, a squared-ReLU feed-forward layer of width 4​d4d, no biases, and untied input and output embeddings. We change only what is held fixed. Schwethelm et al. (2026) hold the executed depth fixed, so that more loops mean fewer unique layers; we hold the unique parameters fixed, as Prairie et al. (2026) do, so that a loop setting changes the compute and not the model. The main grid spans five model sizes, from 58M to 919M non-embedding parameters (Table 4); width and depth grow together, and the recurrent block with the input injection holds 51% of the non-embedding parameters at four sizes and 56% at 120M. Short size names round NN; including the untied input and output embeddings, total parameter counts run from about 107M to about 1.06B. We quote budgets per parameter as D/ND/N. The scaling suite supplements this grid with two compute-matched pairs, adding the 79M and 162M models at one configuration each (Appendix D).

Loop settings and budgets.

The scaling suite spans 1.1–1,291 training tokens per parameter and uses fifteen loop settings. Ten core settings, (1,1)(1,1); (2,1)(2,1) and (2,2)(2,2); (4,1)(4,1), (4,2)(4,2), (4,3)(4,3) and (4,4)(4,4); and (8,2)(8,2), (8,4)(8,4) and (8,8)(8,8), cover T∈{1,2,4,8}T\in\{1,2,4,8\} forward loops, full and truncated BPTT, and ratios B/TB/T from 14\tfrac{1}{4} to 1. Five more settings extend them: (8,1)(8,1), and T=16T=16 with B=1B=1, 4, 8 and 16 at three sizes and short budgets (Sections B.5 and F). The part of the training compute that depends on the loops grows with T+2​BT+2B, since a backward loop costs twice a forward loop (Section C.1); (4,1)(4,1) thus costs as much per token as (2,2)(2,2), and (8,2)(8,2) as much as (4,4)(4,4). Token budgets DD are given in units of D0=230≈1.07×109D_{0}=2^{30}\approx 1.07\times 10^{9} tokens. We group runs by their target token budget; actual token counts may differ slightly because of batch rounding. Predictions use the actual token count DD. An experimental configuration is a choice of (N,D,T,B)(N,D,T,B); a run is one training execution of that configuration. Each configuration contributes one accepted validation loss to the analysis.

Data and evaluation.

We train on the 100B-token sample of FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024), the corpus of the looped scaling study of Lee et al. (2026), in a pre-shuffled release,33 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/karpathy/fineweb-edu-100b-shuffle tokenized with the Llama 2 tokenizer (Touvron et al., 2023) of the reference recipe (Schwethelm et al., 2026) into sequences of 2,048 tokens. We report cross-entropy in nats per token on the last two shards of the release, which no run trains on, after removing the documents whose exact text also appears in the training data (the same web page often occurs in several crawls).

Optimization.

We use the optimizers of the reference recipe (Schwethelm et al., 2026). MuonH, a variant of Muon that keeps each weight matrix at a fixed Frobenius norm (Jordan et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025), trains the hidden weight matrices (attention, feed-forward and input injection), and AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) trains the embedding, output and normalization parameters, both without weight decay. The MuonH update adds 0.06–5.7% to the compute of the forward and backward passes; the analysis leaves it out, and the measured compute we report includes it (Section C.1). The peak learning rates follow the reference’s transfer rule (Schwethelm et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2026), a power law in the batch and training tokens with the token exponent re-estimated for our budgets, and the global batch grows as 64​D/D064\sqrt{D/D_{0}} sequences, following the square-root scaling of the loss-optimal batch in prior work (Li et al., 2025b; Bergsma et al., 2025; Filatov et al., 2025) (Appendix E). The learning rate warms up over the first 2% of steps and decays with a cosine to 10% of its peak; gradients are not clipped.

Runs and compute.

The results in this paper come from 592 training runs with 2.7×10222.7\times 10^{22} FLOPs of training compute, counted as in Section C.1 with the optimizer update. The scaling suite contains 397 runs behind 347 configurations: 385 runs in the five-size grid (Appendix F) and 12 runs in two compute-matched pairs (Appendix D). Each configuration’s loss is the mean of its accepted runs. The remaining 195 distinct runs support the other experiments. These experiments comprise four more runs at 480M in Figure 8, nine further runs of the compute-optimal pairs and the 36 of the untied comparison (Appendix D), and the 66 learning-rate and 124 batch-size runs of Figures 12 and 13; 44 runs belong to two of these groups and are counted once. Counting cancelled runs, runs replaced by reruns, pilot runs and earlier calibration sweeps that the paper does not report, the study trained more than 1,100 runs with about 4.8×10224.8\times 10^{22} FLOPs.

Appendix B The law in detail

This appendix details the measured patterns behind the law, its fit and validation, the bounded gain, and the runs at sixteen loops.

B.1  What the runs show before any law is fitted

The measured losses separate the effects of forward and backward loops without a fitted law (Appendix F). Forward loops that receive no gradient add almost nothing at first: at fixed BB, doubling TT from BB to 2​B2B changes the loss by less than 0.007 nats in all 24 size–budget combinations trained in all ten core settings, while doubling it again, from 2​B2B to 4​B4B, lowers the loss in all 24. Spending the same compute per token on backward loops is better: (2,2)(2,2) beats (4,1)(4,1) and (4,4)(4,4) beats (8,2)(8,2) in all 24, by 0.023 nats on average for (2,2)(2,2) against (4,1)(4,1). Backward loops in turn have diminishing returns: with full BPTT, every doubling of T=BT=B, from 1 to 8, lowers the loss, by less each time, in all 24 combinations where all four settings were trained.

B.2  Empirical looping coefficient

The looping coefficient g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) in (4.1) rescales the recurrent block’s parameter count. To estimate it from the runs, we first find the non-looped model size that matches a looped run’s measured loss at the same token budget. This defines the empirical effective size, which we then convert to a looping coefficient using the run’s parameter counts.

Let d=Dtarget/D0d=D_{\mathrm{target}}/D_{0} denote a target budget level, where DtargetD_{\mathrm{target}} is the target token count and D0=230D_{0}=2^{30} tokens. At each dd, we collect the accepted non-looped (T,B)=(1,1)(T,B)=(1,1) configurations and order their actual parameter counts and measured losses as (nj,ℓj)j=1md(n_{j},\ell_{j})_{j=1}^{m_{d}}, where n1<⋯<nmdn_{1}<\cdots<n_{m_{d}}. Each configuration contributes its accepted loss once, following the same aggregation rules as the scaling-law fit. We require at least three distinct sizes and strictly decreasing losses, ℓ1>⋯>ℓmd\ell_{1}>\cdots>\ell_{m_{d}}, as holds for the eligible reference groups. We interpolate log size as a function of loss:

ϕd​(ℓ)≔PCHIP⁡[(ℓj,log⁡nj)j=md,…,1]​(ℓ),ℓ∈[ℓmd,ℓ1].\phi_{d}(\ell)\coloneqq\operatorname{PCHIP}\!\left[(\ell_{j},\log n_{j})_{j=m_{d},\ldots,1}\right](\ell),\qquad\ell\in[\ell_{m_{d}},\ell_{1}]. (B.1)

Here PCHIP denotes shape-preserving piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation (Fritsch and Butland, 1984), with reference points ordered by increasing loss. The interpolant in (B.1) passes through each measured point, ϕd​(ℓj)=log⁡nj\phi_{d}(\ell_{j})=\log n_{j}, and preserves monotonicity between points. This loss-to-size conversion uses only the non-looped measurements, independent of the fitted coefficients of (4.1).

For a looped configuration ii, let LiL_{i} be its measured loss, did_{i} its target budget, and Nonce,i,Nrec,i>0N_{\mathrm{once},i},N_{\mathrm{rec},i}>0 its once-run and recurrent counts; when its reference group is eligible and Li∈[ℓmdi,ℓ1]L_{i}\in[\ell_{m_{d_{i}}},\ell_{1}], define

Nwidehateff,i≔exp⁡[ϕdi​(Li)],gwidehati≔Nwidehateff,i−Nonce,iNrec,i.\widehat{N}_{\mathrm{eff},i}\coloneqq\exp\!\bigl[\phi_{d_{i}}(L_{i})\bigr],\qquad\widehat{g}_{i}\coloneqq\frac{\widehat{N}_{\mathrm{eff},i}-N_{\mathrm{once},i}}{N_{\mathrm{rec},i}}. (B.2)

In (B.2), we subtract the once-run parameters and divide by the recurrent block’s size, as in (4.1). Each empirical coefficient depends on the run’s size and token budget; g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) is the law’s shared prediction. We report an estimate only when the reference group is eligible and the measured loss lies within its observed range, without extrapolation. Budget matching uses the target level dd, keeping batch-rounded budgets in the same group. Actual consumed tokens differ from the target token budget by less than 0.2%0.2\% in these runs; we leave these differences uncorrected.

For example, the 239.24M non-embedding-parameter run at T=B=2T=B=2 and D=4​D0D=4D_{0} has loss 2.42722.4272 nats per token. The reference interpolation gives Nwidehateff=345.20\widehat{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}=345.20M, hence gwidehat=(345.20−117.98)/121.26≃1.874\widehat{g}=(345.20-117.98)/121.26\simeq 1.874, using its own once-run and recurrent counts in millions of parameters.

For each setting (T,B)(T,B), let ℐT,B\mathcal{I}_{T,B} be the set of eligible size–budget configurations. Figure 3 shows the median of {gwidehati:i∈ℐT,B}\{\widehat{g}_{i}:i\in\mathcal{I}_{T,B}\}, with the 25th and 75th percentiles as the interquartile range. Configurations have equal weight; for sorted estimates x(1),…,x(n)x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(n)}, a percentile at probability uu linearly interpolates adjacent order statistics at rank 1+(n−1)​u1+(n-1)u. Figure 6 uses the same loss-matched estimates, with total-size ratios shown where indicated. The surface figure includes 163 eligible configurations with T≤8T\leq 8: 121 from the fitting set and 42 from the separately held-out set. Reference configurations may also come from either set, and estimates that use the same references are dependent. These figures therefore describe agreement with the runs rather than independent validation of the law. The interquartile ranges show variation across sizes and budgets, not confidence intervals. Section B.3 reports the separate holdout evaluations in loss units.

Figure 3 uses the same estimator on the 150 eligible configurations with T∈{2,4,8}T\in\{2,4,8\} and 1/4≤r=B/T≤11/4\leq r=B/T\leq 1. Markers show medians and bars show minima and maxima. For each TT, we fit an intercept aTa_{T} and slope sTs_{T} by ordinary least squares with equal weight per cell:

(awidehatT,swidehatT)=arg​mina,s∑i:Ti=T[a+slog2ri−log2gwidehati]2.(\widehat{a}_{T},\widehat{s}_{T})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a,s}\sum_{i:T_{i}=T}\left[a+s\log_{2}r_{i}-\log_{2}\widehat{g}_{i}\right]^{2}. (B.3)

In (B.3), the fitted slopes are 0.8230.823, 0.4460.446 and 0.1730.173 for T=2,4,8T=2,4,8, respectively; these lines summarize the empirical trend across the 150 configurations rather than a separate scaling law.

B.3  Form and fit

The looping coefficient is

g⁡(T,B)=exp⁡[c⁡(1−T−p​B−q)],Neff=Nonce+g⁡(T,B)​Nrec.g(T,B)=\exp[c(1-T^{-p}B^{-q})],\qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}=N_{\mathrm{once}}+g(T,B)N_{\mathrm{rec}}. (B.4)

The normalization is exact: g⁡(1,1)=1g(1,1)=1, so (T,B)=(1,1)(T,B)=(1,1) gives Neff=NN_{\mathrm{eff}}=N. For c,p,q>0c,p,q>0, g⁡(T,B)g(T,B) increases in TT and in BB toward ece^{c}. The fitted ceiling of the looping coefficient is ec≃3.04e^{c}\simeq 3.04; it is an extrapolation, not an observed asymptotic limit. With full BPTT the looping coefficient is g⁡(T,T)=exp⁡[c⁡(1−T−(p+q))]g(T,T)=\exp[c(1-T^{-(p+q)})]; for B<TB<T it is smaller by the factor exp⁡[−c​T−(p+q)​(r−q−1)]\exp[-cT^{-(p+q)}(r^{-q}-1)], r=B/Tr=B/T, which approaches one as TT grows.

We split the 347 scaling-suite configurations into 230 for fitting and 117 for testing. The fitting set spans fifteen loop settings and includes 226 configurations from the five-size grid, covering five model sizes at approximately 9, 18, 37, or 74 training tokens per parameter, giving the sizes a common budget range. Of these 226 configurations, 194 use the eleven settings with at most eight loops (a few at the largest budgets were not run) and 32 use T=16T=16. The other four fitting configurations are also used to compare a looped model with a non-looped model at each of two training-compute budgets (Appendix D), adding sizes 79M and 162M to the grid’s five sizes. Each configuration enters once through the mean loss of its accepted runs, aggregating repeated runs and seeds and removing duplicate exports. The other 117 configurations of the scaling suite, mostly at shorter or longer budgets, enter no fit and serve as separate tests. Predictions use actual consumed tokens and exact architecture parameter counts. The fixed normalizations are N0=2.4×108N_{0}=2.4\times 10^{8} and D0=230D_{0}=2^{30}.

We minimize equally weighted squared residuals in nats per token. All nine coefficients are refitted on every training fold using 64 independent uniform random starts, retaining the lowest-cost converged solution. The trust-region reflective solver uses an analytic Jacobian, Jacobian scaling, at most 4000 evaluations, and tolerances ftol=xtol=gtol=10−12\mathrm{ftol}=\mathrm{xtol}=\mathrm{gtol}=10^{-12}. Seeds are 20261010 plus the deterministic fold index. No full-data coefficients initialize a held-out fold, and no learned preprocessing, weighting or hyperparameter tuning is used.

In optimization coordinates, E∈[0,3]E\in[0,3], log⁡A,log⁡H∈[−10,15]\log A,\log H\in[-10,15], α,β,κ∈[0.01,3]\alpha,\beta,\kappa\in[0.01,3], p,q∈[0.001,10]p,q\in[0.001,10], and log⁡c∈[log⁡0.001,log⁡10]\log c\in[\log 0.001,\log 10]. Initial ranges are E∈[0.3,1.2]E\in[0.3,1.2], log⁡A,log⁡H∈[0.5,2.5]\log A,\log H\in[0.5,2.5], α,β∈[0.25,0.65]\alpha,\beta\in[0.25,0.65], κ∈[0.15,0.45]\kappa\in[0.15,0.45], p,q∈[0.1,2]p,q\in[0.1,2], and log⁡c∈[log⁡0.2,log⁡2]\log c\in[\log 0.2,\log 2]. The power-law gain of Section B.4 uses the same ranges for the first six coefficients and ϕT,ϕB∈[−5,5]\phi_{T},\phi_{B}\in[-5,5], initialized in [0.05,0.8][0.05,0.8]. All 264 fits of each law converge with full-rank Jacobians (the largest-size holdout reaches E=0E=0).

Validation and aggregation.

Residuals are prediction minus measurement. Point LOO holds out one entire accepted configuration. Size folds hold out all combinations at the selected model size. Budget folds group the target level Dtarget/D0D_{\mathrm{target}}/D_{0}, retaining batch-rounded versions together. Setting folds hold out an entire (T,B)(T,B) pair. Each family covers all 230 configurations. Point LOO trains on 229 configurations and tests on the remaining one, repeating this for all 230. Table 9 reports pooled errors, which weight held-out configurations equally. Every fold converges and none is dropped. Appendix F overlays the law on the 226 fitted grid configurations; the four fitted configurations from the compute-matched pairs are not shown there.

B.4  Why a bounded gain

Prior scaling laws for looped models let the looping gain grow as a power of the loop count, TϕT^{\phi} (Schwethelm et al., 2026). We extend this form to TϕT​BϕBT^{\phi_{T}}B^{\phi_{B}} in place of g⁡(T,B)g(T,B), keeping the rest of (4.1) unchanged. This form is the limit of our gain as c→∞c\to\infty with c​p→ϕTcp\to\phi_{T} and c​q→ϕBcq\to\phi_{B}; under full BPTT it reduces to TϕT^{\phi} with ϕ=ϕT+ϕB\phi=\phi_{T}+\phi_{B}. We fit both laws on the same configurations, folds and solver. The power-law gain is less accurate in every evaluation in Table 10, with nearly twice the error on a held-out (T,B)(T,B) setting (1.65×10−21.65\times 10^{-2} vs. 8.67×10−38.67\times 10^{-3} nats); it keeps growing where the runs level off, and held out at sixteen loops its error is three times that of the bounded gain (Section B.5). Our gain rises from g⁡(1,1)=1g(1,1)=1 toward ece^{c}; with full BPTT and p+q=1p+q=1 it is the reciprocal exponential gain exp⁡[c⁡(1−1/T)]\exp[c(1-1/T)], and free exponents separate the ceiling from the rate of approach.

The derivatives distinguish the empirical assumption from its algebraic consequences. At fixed coefficients, with s=p+qs=p+q, the total derivatives below follow the full-BPTT path B=TB=T:

∂log⁡g∂T\displaystyle\frac{\partial\log g}{\partial T} =cpT−p−1B−q>0,∂log⁡g∂B=cqT−pB−q−1>0,\displaystyle=cpT^{-p-1}B^{-q}>0,\qquad\frac{\partial\log g}{\partial B}=cqT^{-p}B^{-q-1}>0, (B.5)
dd​T​g​(T,T)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}T}g(T,T) =c​s​T−s−1​g​(T,T)>0,\displaystyle=csT^{-s-1}g(T,T)>0,
d2d​T2​g​(T,T)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}T^{2}}g(T,T) =c​s​T−s−2​g​(T,T)​[c​s​T−s−(s+1)].\displaystyle=csT^{-s-2}g(T,T)\,[csT^{-s}-(s+1)].

For the fitted coefficients, c​s<s+1cs<s+1, so the full-BPTT gain is concave for T≥1T\geq 1. Concavity is not automatic for every positive parameter choice. The effective size is an equivalence in validation loss, not in stored knowledge (Zhu et al., 2025).

B.5  Runs at sixteen loops

The fit contains 32 configurations at T=16T=16, across 120M, 240M and 480M, with backward counts 1, 4, 8 and 16 and target token budgets from 2​D02D_{0} to 8​D08D_{0}. Holding out this whole row leaves 198 training configurations and gives RMSE 0.0115 nats, against 0.0340 for the power-law gain of prior work, which keeps growing beyond the loop counts it is fitted on. The harder extrapolation is the row without looping, T=1T=1: RMSE 0.0172 (0.0207 for the power-law gain), the largest forward-row error. The four sixteen-loop configurations of 480M at 2​D02D_{0} lie outside the fitting set.

Appendix C Training compute and allocation

We first define the training-compute cost, then discuss the fixed-size switch points and their experimental checks. Section C.4 gives the allocation derivations for prescribed forward loops, joint loop counts, and fixed or free model size.

C.1  Training compute

Training compute counts the FLOPs of the forward and backward passes. We use the usual convention of 2 FLOPs per parameter and token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). The prelude and coda run forward and backward once per token. Each forward loop runs the recurrent block forward once, and each backward loop adds a backward pass through it, which costs twice as much. The compute of the passes per token, using the approximately equal parameter split, is

F⁡(T,B)≈N⁡(3+T+2​B)+Fattn​(T,B)+Fout,F(T,B)\;\approx\;N\,(3+T+2B)+F_{\mathrm{attn}}(T,B)+F_{\mathrm{out}}, (C.1)

where FattnF_{\mathrm{attn}} counts the attention products of every executed layer and FoutF_{\mathrm{out}} the output projection.44 4 We use actual layer counts for numerical compute accounting. Each transformer layer has 12​d212d^{2} matrix parameters and input injection has 2​d22d^{2}, so the exact matrix contribution under our counting convention is 72​d2​(ℓp+ℓc)+4​d2​(T+2​B)​(6​ℓr+1)72d^{2}(\ell_{p}+\ell_{c})+4d^{2}(T+2B)(6\ell_{r}+1). With width dd, sequence length SS and vocabulary size VV (32,064 with padding): Fattn=4​S​d​[ 3​(ℓp+ℓc)+(T+2​B)​ℓr]F_{\mathrm{attn}}=4Sd\,[\,3(\ell_{p}+\ell_{c})+(T+2B)\,\ell_{r}\,] and Fout=6​V​dF_{\mathrm{out}}=6Vd. Embedding lookup, normalization, and activations are omitted. The attention products of the recurrent block follow the same count, one unit per forward loop and two more per backward loop, so every loop-dependent term grows with T+2​BT+2B, as in the accounting of truncated BPTT by Prairie et al. (2026) and Schwethelm et al. (2026); for a given model, (2,2)(2,2) and (4,1)(4,1) therefore cost the same per token, as do (4,4)(4,4) and (8,2)(8,2).

For a model of size NN we write this compute per token as FN​(T,B)=uN+vN​(T+2​B)F_{N}(T,B)=u_{N}+v_{N}(T+2B), where uNu_{N} collects the prelude, coda and output and vN>0v_{N}>0 one forward pass through the recurrent block with its attention, so that DD training tokens cost

C≃FN​(T,B)​D.C\;\simeq\;F_{N}(T,B)\,D. (C.2)

At fixed NN and DD, the compute depends on the loop counts only through T+2​BT+2B. (5.1) is its leading term, without the attention and output costs.

The optimizer update is negligible.

MuonH also spends FLOPs on each update: five Newton–Schulz iterations per weight matrix (Jordan et al., 2024), a cost FoptF_{\mathrm{opt}} per step that depends on the model but not on TT or BB, so that a run of nstepn_{\mathrm{step}} steps costs

C=F⁡(T,B)​D+Fopt​nstep.C\;=\;F(T,B)\,D+F_{\mathrm{opt}}\,n_{\mathrm{step}}. (C.3)

Across our runs the update adds 0.06–5.7% to the compute of the passes. It cannot change the split between forward and backward loops, since it does not depend on either; leaving it out moves the fixed-size switch points of Section 6.1 by less than 0.5%, and it gives the models with more trainable parameters, the untied model and the model without looping at its compute-optimal size, 0.5–0.75% more compute, or about 0.001 nats in loss (Appendix D). Like prior scaling studies (Schwethelm et al., 2026; Prairie et al., 2026), our analysis therefore omits it and uses (C.2); the measured compute in figures, tables and Section A.2 includes it unless stated otherwise.

C.2  Switch points

At a fixed size, each setting traces a loss curve in CC, and the best setting at each compute lies on their lower envelope (Table 12). Full BPTT reaches the envelope almost everywhere: among all fifteen trained settings, four of them with T=16T=16, the best setting at every compute is (1,1)(1,1), (2,2)(2,2), (4,4)(4,4), (8,8)(8,8) or (16,16)(16,16), apart from a narrow compute range between (2,2)(2,2) and (4,4)(4,4) where (4,3)(4,3) leads by at most 0.002 nats on our integer menu (Section 6.1). Truncation lowers the compute per token but gives up the gain of the loops it does not train, and at equal compute per token a setting that trains all of its fewer loops is the better buy, as the runs show directly (Section B.1). Measured in the tokens per parameter that the model without looping trains on at the same compute, two loops become the best choice at about 14–17, four overtake two at about 312–413, and eight overtake four at about 7,000–9,600 (sixteen pay only beyond 147,000–210,000).

C.3  The runs at a fixed size

The runs confirm the first switch and the role of the trained loops (Figure 8; Figure 1c previews the 120M slice). Beyond about 30 tokens per parameter, (2,2)(2,2) ends below the model without looping at every point we measured, by about 0.01 nats at 50 tokens per parameter and by 0.025 at 200. Loops without gradient do not win: (4,1)(4,1), which costs as much per token as (2,2)(2,2) but trains only one of its four loops, stays above the model without looping up to 200 tokens per parameter. At 60M, 120M and 240M, where the runs reach several hundred tokens per parameter, (4,4)(4,4) overtakes (2,2)(2,2), as the law predicts, but already at about 200 tokens per parameter rather than at the law’s 374–413. At one compute per size far into this range, that of (4,4)(4,4) at 32​D032D_{0} for 60M and 240M and at 24​D024D_{0} for 120M (1,291, 533 and 335 tokens per parameter of the model without looping), the runs read 2.514, 2.389 and 2.247 for the model without looping, 2.479, 2.358 and 2.223 for (2,2)(2,2), and 2.460, 2.345 and 2.218 for (4,4)(4,4): (4,4)(4,4) is the lowest, 0.019, 0.012 and 0.006 nats below (2,2)(2,2), while (4,3)(4,3) at the same compute trails (4,4)(4,4) by 0.010, 0.008 and 0.006 and (8,8)(8,8) lies above it at all three sizes. At 480M the same compute is reached at 174 tokens per parameter, before the switch: the model without looping reads 2.141, (2,2)(2,2) 2.121 and (4,4)(4,4) 2.124, so (2,2)(2,2) and (4,4)(4,4) are level and both stay below the model without looping. The runs with T=16T=16, trained at 2​D02D_{0}–8​D08D_{0} (Section B.5), lie well below the compute where eight or sixteen loops pay and stay above (4,4)(4,4) at equal compute.

C.4  Allocation identities and their assumptions

We follow the allocation regimes of Sections 5.1 to 6.2: first prescribe TT, then optimize the split between T,BT,B, and finally allocate loops, data, and model size. The prescribed-TT and free-size results use the leading matrix-FLOP approximation (5.1); the joint-loop and fixed-size calculations use (C.2), with the attention and output costs. All omit the optimizer update (Section C.1).

C.4.1  Fixed forward-loop count: optimize size, data, and backward loops

Lemma C.1 (Optimal backward-loop allocation).

Fix the integer forward-loop count T≥1T\geq 1 and training-compute budget C>0C>0. Suppose the loss follows (4.1), with positive fitted coefficients E,A,H,α,β,κ,c,p,qE,A,H,\alpha,\beta,\kappa,c,p,q and normalization scales N0,D0>0N_{0},D_{0}>0. Let N=Nonce+NrecN=N_{\mathrm{once}}+N_{\mathrm{rec}} be the parameter count. Since L=E+JκL=E+J^{\kappa} with κ>0\kappa>0, minimizing LL is equivalent to minimizing JJ; eliminating yy gives

C.4.2  Joint forward–backward allocation at equal compute

Lemma C.2 (Optimal joint forward–backward allocation).

Fix an architecture with Nrec>0N_{\mathrm{rec}}>0 and a token count D>0D>0. Suppose the loss follows (4.1), with positive fitted coefficients E,A,H,α,β,κE,A,H,\alpha,\beta,\kappa, c,p,qc,p,q and positive normalization scales N0,D0N_{0},D_{0}. Let TT and BB be continuous variables. For any S≥3S\geq 3, consider the equal-compute problem under (C.2):

minimizeT,B∈ℝL⁡(N,D,T,B)subject toT+2​B=S,1≤B≤T.\underset{T,B\in\mathbb{R}}{\operatorname{minimize}}\quad L(N,D,T,B)\qquad\text{subject to}\quad T+2B=S,\qquad 1\leq B\leq T. (C.16)

If q≥2​pq\geq 2p, its unique solution is T∗=B∗=S/3T^{*}=B^{*}=S/3, corresponding to full BPTT.

Proof.

At fixed architecture and token count, (C.2) depends on the loop counts only through S=T+2​BS=T+2B, including the attention products. Thus every feasible split has the same compute. Since the loss is strictly decreasing in NeffN_{\mathrm{eff}} and Nrec>0N_{\mathrm{rec}}>0, minimizing it is equivalent to maximizing g⁡(T,B)g(T,B). Using g⁡(T,B)=exp⁡[c⁡(1−T−p​B−q)]g(T,B)=\exp[c(1-T^{-p}B^{-q})] with c>0c>0, this is equivalent to minimizing T−p​B−qT^{-p}B^{-q}, or its logarithm. Substituting T=S−2​BT=S-2B gives 1≤B≤S/31\leq B\leq S/3 and the strictly convex objective

h⁡(B)=−p​log⁡(S−2​B)−q​log⁡B,h′′​(B)=4​p(S−2​B)2+qB2>0.h(B)=-p\log(S-2B)-q\log B,\qquad h^{\prime\prime}(B)=\frac{4p}{(S-2B)^{2}}+\frac{q}{B^{2}}>0. (C.17)

When q≥2​pq\geq 2p, the constraint B≤TB\leq T gives

h′​(B)=2​pT−qB≤2​p−qT≤0.h^{\prime}(B)=\frac{2p}{T}-\frac{q}{B}\leq\frac{2p-q}{T}\leq 0. (C.18)

The derivative is strictly negative whenever B<TB<T, including when q=2​pq=2p. Hence the unique minimum is at B=S/3B=S/3, where T=BT=B. For S=3S=3, this is also the only feasible split. ∎

The replacement preserves N,DN,D and strictly improves any truncated setting, so the conclusion also holds when either or both are optimized, provided the replacement is admissible. It does not require fixed parameter proportions across model sizes. Including the optimizer update does not change the result, since its cost is independent of T,BT,B.

The condition is stronger than q>pq>p: a backward loop costs twice a forward loop, so the comparison is qq versus 2​p2p. Our adopted fit satisfies q>2​pq>2p. For integer or restricted loop menus, S/3S/3 may be unavailable, so the continuous dominance argument does not replace the discrete check (C.19).

Lemma C.4 (Asymptotic loop–token allocation).

Suppose the loss follows (4.1), with positive fitted coefficients E,A,H,α,β,κ,c,p,qE,A,H,\alpha,\beta,\kappa,c,p,q and positive normalization scales N0,D0N_{0},D_{0}. Moreover, T∗​(C)→∞T^{*}(C)\to\infty as C→∞C\to\infty: for any fixed M≥1M\geq 1, every T≤MT\leq M has J⁡(T,N,C)≥X⁡(M)J(T;N,C)\geq X(M), whereas J⁡(2​M,N,C)→X⁡(2​M)<X⁡(M)J(2M;N,C)\to X(2M)<X(M). Writing s=p+qs=p+q, the large-TT limits are

Neff′\displaystyle N_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\prime} ∼NreccsecT−s−1,FN(T,T)∼3vNT.\displaystyle\sim N_{\mathrm{rec}}cse^{c}T^{-s-1},\qquad F_{N}(T,T)\sim 3v_{N}T.

The bracket in (C.23) is thus asymptotic to a positive constant times Tβ−1​Ts+1=Tβ+sT^{\beta-1}T^{s+1}=T^{\beta+s}, so C⁡(T)C(T) is asymptotic to a positive constant times T(β+s)/βT^{(\beta+s)/\beta}. Evaluating this relation at T∗​(C)T^{*}(C) and inverting gives the first part of (C.28), and D∗​(C)∼C/(3​vN​T∗​(C))D^{*}(C)\sim C/(3v_{N}T^{*}(C)) gives the second, recovering (6.3). ∎

The current coefficients give exponents approximately 0.238 and 0.762 ((6.4) rounds them to 0.24 and 0.76). The dominance argument above applies within this law and compute model; its extrapolation to unbounded depth is not empirically established. For (2,2)(2,2), Neff≃1.462​NN_{\mathrm{eff}}\simeq 1.462N, Ncomp≃1.507​NN_{\mathrm{comp}}\simeq 1.507N and χ≃1.031\chi\simeq 1.031, so (C.31) predicts equal loss at 3.1% more compute and 31.6% fewer parameters than (1,1)(1,1).

For (2,2)(2,2) the bracketed multiplier is about 1.72×10−31.72\times 10^{-3}, or 0.172% of the non-looped model’s excess loss above EE, rather than a constant gap in nats, making the compute convention consequential.

Limits of the scale-independent ratios.

The identities describe an empirical loss law under a specified compute approximation; they do not establish a universal property of looped models. Size or data bounds can put an optimum on a boundary. A size-dependent recurrent share or the attention, output, and optimizer terms breaks the simple 6​χ​Neff​D6\chi N_{\mathrm{eff}}D factorization. Full-compute optimization therefore requires an explicit architectural scaling family and a fresh numerical envelope. Its results should be reported separately from the analytic ratios, using the same adopted fit.

Appendix D Compute-optimal pairs and the untied model

The main text (Section 6.3) compares (2,2)(2,2) with a compute-optimal model without looping while allowing model size and token count to vary. Below we give the full table for that comparison, followed by a controlled comparison at fixed tokens against an untied model with a separate block per loop.

Compute-optimal pairs.

We trained (1,1)(1,1) and (2,2)(2,2) each at the size and token count that minimize its loss for the same training compute, with three seeds each (Table 13). The first two pairs also belong to the scaling suite and its fitting set. At all three budgets, the looped model has 27–32% fewer non-embedding parameters and comes within (1​–​8)×10−3(1\text{--}8)\times 10^{-3} nats of the model without looping. At 2.1×10192.1\times 10^{19} FLOPs (2.0×10192.0\times 10^{19} for the forward and backward passes alone), training the 344M (2,2)(2,2) model on 8% more tokens, and so with 8% more compute, lowers its loss to 2.3590, (7.3±1.8)×10−3(7.3\pm 1.8)\times 10^{-3} nats below the 471M model without looping (Figure 1d).

The untied model.

The untied model of a looped model is the same network in which each loop has its own copy of the recurrent block, input injection and normalization. For two loops it holds Nonce+2​NrecN_{\mathrm{once}}+2N_{\mathrm{rec}} parameters, about 1.5 times as many, at the same compute per token. Tying layers to save parameters goes back to ALBERT (Lan et al., 2019), and Bae et al. (2025a) relax the tie of looped models converted from pretrained ones. Each copy is initialized like the looped model; with all copies set equal, the untied model reproduces the looped model’s loss and logits exactly.

Design and results.

Each size trains at about 18 tokens per parameter of the looped model, close to the compute-optimal ratio of Hoffmann et al. (2022): 60M at D0D_{0}, 120M at 2​D02D_{0}, 240M at 4​D04D_{0} and 480M at 8​D08D_{0}, with the recipe of its (2,2)(2,2) run and three seeds per model. Alongside the untied model, we train (2,2)(2,2) at the same width and (2,2)(2,2) widened to about 80% of the untied model’s non-embedding parameters, on the same tokens (Table 14). At the untied model’s width the looped model trails by 9×10−39\times 10^{-3}–1.7×10−21.7\times 10^{-2} nats (1.3×10−21.3\times 10^{-2} averaged over the four sizes), against (3​–​4)×10−3(3\text{--}4)\times 10^{-3} by the law, whose error at these (2,2)(2,2) runs is at most 4×10−34\times 10^{-3} nats. The wider looped model uses 15–22% more forward-and-backward compute per token than the untied model and reaches a lower loss by 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}–1.7×10−21.7\times 10^{-2} nats, in all twelve seed pairs.

Appendix E Learning rate and batch size

Our runs follow one learning-rate rule and one batch-size rule, both set by the token budget DD (Table 15). We test each rule against sweeps that vary only the learning rate or only the batch; a learning-rate sweep scales the MuonH and AdamW learning rates by one common factor. We call a value acceptable when its loss is within 0.25% of the optimum of its sweep, about a tenth of what (4,4)(4,4) gains over (1,1)(1,1) at the same model size and budget.

Learning-rate rule.

We take the transfer rule of the reference recipe (Schwethelm et al., 2026) for the peak MuonH learning rate of the hidden weight matrices,

η= 0.014​(b128)0.558​(DDref)−γ,Dref=9.83×108,\eta\;=\;0.014\,\Bigl(\frac{b}{128}\Bigr)^{0.558}\Bigl(\frac{D}{D_{\mathrm{ref}}}\Bigr)^{-\gamma},\qquad D_{\mathrm{ref}}=9.83\times 10^{8}, (E.1)

where bb is the global batch in sequences of 2,048 tokens; the AdamW learning rates scale with width, and those of the embedding and output also with batch. The reference recipe uses the token exponent γ=0.32\gamma=0.32 of HyperP (Ren et al., 2026), a transfer rule for MuonH. On our models this exponent is too small: relative to (E.1) with γ=0.32\gamma=0.32, the optimal learning rate keeps falling as DD grows (Figure 12b). We thus re-estimate γ\gamma and, as our models vary in depth, test for a depth term.

Token exponent: γ=0.40\gamma=0.40.

We swept the learning rate at the smallest and the largest model size, 60M at D0D_{0}, 4​D04D_{0} and 16​D016D_{0} and 1B at 4​D04D_{0} and 16​D016D_{0}, each with (4,4)(4,4) and (4,1)(4,1), and fit a quadratic in log⁡η\log\eta to each sweep to locate its optimum (Figure 12a). The exponent that minimizes the rule’s largest loss above the optimum is γ=0.406\gamma=0.406 (95% interval 0.400–0.412), and we use γ=0.40\gamma=0.40. The rule is then within 0.06% of the optimum in every sweep, the largest gap being 60M with (4,1)(4,1) at 16​D016D_{0}, whereas γ=0.32\gamma=0.32 ends up 0.45% above the optimum at 1B and 16​D016D_{0}.

No depth correction.

Depth-wise transfer rules lower the learning rate as networks get deeper (Yang et al., 2023; Bordelon et al., 2023; Dey et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026). For updates normalized as in MuonH, keeping the change of the network per step fixed requires η∝ℓ−1/2\eta\propto\ell^{-1/2} with residual branches scaled by ℓ−1/2\ell^{-1/2}, or η∝ℓ−1\eta\propto\ell^{-1} without that scaling, where ℓ\ell is the number of executed layers (Ren et al., 2026, Theorem 3). Our recipe scales neither the residual branches nor the learning rate with depth, although our models get deeper both with size (20 to 40 executed layers from 60M to 1B at T=4T=4) and with the number of forward loops (12 to 36 at 60M). Yet the optimum does not follow the depth (Figure 12c–d): at D0D_{0}, the rule’s learning rate is the best of 1/21/\sqrt{2}, 1 and 2\sqrt{2} times itself in all six sweeps, and the fitted optima stay within about 7% of the rule, where the trend HyperP measures without residual scaling would lower them by more than half. The optimal learning rate follows the training tokens, not the depth, so the rule needs no depth term.

Batch-size rule.

We set the global batch to

b⁡(D)= 64​D/D0​sequences,b(D)\;=\;64\sqrt{D/D_{0}}\ \text{sequences}, (E.2)

rounded to a ladder whose neighboring steps differ by about 2\sqrt{2} (…\dots, 32, 48, 64, 88, 128, 176, 256, 352). The loss-optimal batch grows about as D\sqrt{D}, as in prior work (Li et al., 2025b; Bergsma et al., 2025; Filatov et al., 2025), and in eleven batch sweeps with (4,4)(4,4) (60M at five budgets, 240M and 1B at three) the rule’s batch is acceptable in every one (Figure 13a).

Prefactor.

The loss is flat over about a factor of two in batch, so the prefactor is a choice between neighboring ladder steps. One step lower, 45​D/D045\sqrt{D/D_{0}}, suits 1B with full BPTT as well as 64 suits 60M, but truncated BPTT prefers larger batches: at 1B and 16​D016D_{0}, the best batch is 176 for (4,4)(4,4) and 352 for (4,1)(4,1). Over all 33 sweeps with at least three batch sizes, which cover all ten core settings, only the rule is acceptable everywhere: it stays within 0.17% of the best batch, while one step lower reaches 0.30% and one step higher 0.42% (Figure 13b). The rule therefore changes comparisons between loop settings by less than 0.004 nats.

Appendix F The law across the five-size grid

Figure 14 shows the validation loss of the 343 configurations in the suite’s five-size grid, one panel per loop setting. Filled markers denote the 226 configurations used to fit the law of Section 4; open markers denote the rest. The suite’s four fitted configurations from the compute-matched pairs (120M, 79M, 240M and 162M) are listed in Table 13 and are not drawn here. The figure contains 290 configurations in the ten core settings, 17 with (8,1)(8,1) and 36 with T=16T=16. Each configuration shows the mean loss of its accepted runs (385 in all; Section A.2); the law is drawn over each size’s measured budgets. The configurations span 1.1 to 1,291 tokens per parameter, while the fitted ones span 9 to 74. Per loop setting, the law’s RMSE on the fitted configurations is 0.0031 to 0.0093 nats; on the rest it is 0.0200, as most lie below 5 or above 125 tokens per parameter (Section 7). Figure 4 shows the four full-BPTT settings at the 26 size–budget pairs where all four were trained: one set of coefficients tracks all four, with RMSE 0.0053 nats over the 68 fitted configurations (0.0148 over the 36 others).

Appendix G Training curves

Figure 15 shows the training curves of the 385 runs behind the 343 configurations of Appendix F, one panel per loop setting. Each curve is the training loss of every tenth step, the cross-entropy of that step’s batch, against the training compute spent so far, counted as in Section C.1 with the optimizer update; it is not the validation loss on held-out documents that we report (Section A.2). Each token budget is a separate run whose cosine schedule ends at that budget, so a run reaches its final loss only at its end. The dotted line therefore joins run ends only, those that end below every run with less compute, and needs no fit. As in the training-curve envelopes of Hoffmann et al. (2022, Figure A5), larger models take over this frontier as compute grows; at the highest compute of each panel it follows the largest model trained in that setting, 1B, or 480M for T=16T=16.
